• Global average sea level rose roughly 6 inches through the 20th century, and the rate of change has accelerated in recent years. When averaged over all of the world’s oceans, sea level rose at an average rate of 0.06 inches per year from 1880 to 2013. Since 1993, however, average sea level has risen at a rate of 0.12 inches per year—roughly twice as fast as the long-term trend.
  • Even if the world takes robust steps to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, sea level is expected to keep rising for many decades as the oceans, which are slow to warm, continue to absorb heat from the atmosphere.[1] However, the exact amount of sea level rise will still be influenced by future emissions. The lower sea level rise scenario shown here is based on sea level increasing worldwide by half a meter from 2000 to 2100. This scenario is closest to what climate modeling suggests will occur in the intermediate emissions scenario used in other pairings. The higher scenario represents a 1-meter rise from 2000 to 2100 and is most closely linked to the very high emissions scenario used in other pairings.
  • Sea level rose relative to much of the U.S. coastline between 1960 and 2023, particularly the Mid-Atlantic coast and parts of the Gulf coast, where the land is sinking and some stations recorded increases of more than 10 inches. Meanwhile, sea level relative to the coast decreased at some locations in Alaska and the Pacific Northwest where local land elevation has increased due to geologic factors.
  • Projections show sea level continuing to rise at all U.S. coastal locations except for a few in Alaska, where regional geological forces are causing the land to rise more quickly than sea level.
  • There is a possibility that sea level could increase by much more than the amounts shown here. NOAA’s projections also include two higher sea level rise scenarios that could occur if Greenland and Antarctica undergo “rapid ice melt” or partial collapse.[2] Events like these are plausible but difficult to predict.
